summary: Cut-leaf teasel is a tall, very prickly plant that can grow up to about 3 meters (10 feet) tall. Large stands form a dense, tall layer above shorter plants, and can sharply reduce the number of plant species in an area. In New Jersey it has invaded limestone fens and caused rare plants, including the globally rare globe flower, to decline or disappear there. A large plant can make more than 2,000 seeds, and often 80% or more of them can sprout.
history: Cut-leaf teasel is native to temperate Europe and Asia and has been known in the United States since the 1800s. It is sometimes sold for gardens and for dried flower arrangements. It is not as common as common teasel.
seasons: It lives for one or more years as a low rosette of leaves, then flowers once and dies after setting seed. Its rosettes stay green in early spring and late fall, when many native plants are dormant.

handling.text: Mowing does not control it and often makes patches bigger, because mowing equipment spreads the seeds. Small rosettes can be dug up, but plants often resprout if any root is left. Flower stalks can be cut after flowering starts but before seeds form; the cut stalks must be taken away, because seeds can still ripen on them. Getting rid of it from a natural area can take five or six years of work.

report:
New York's official database for invasive species sightings is iMapInvasives, run by the New York Natural Heritage Program (a partnership between SUNY ESF and the NYS Department of Environmental Conservation). You can make a free account and report directly to the online database, which is the preferred method, or use the iMapInvasives mobile app for iPhone and Android, which can upload your records once you have a connection again. If you don't want an account, the site has a public report form; those reports are reviewed by Natural Heritage Program staff each week before being added.

In New York City parks, report what you find instead of removing it yourself. NYC Parks rules forbid cutting, killing or removing any plants, flowers, shrubs or other vegetation without permission from the Parks Commissioner, and forbid chasing, harassing, harming or removing any animal, nest, or the eggs of any amphibian, reptile or bird (56 RCNY §1-04).
